sources.source: Google Cloud: Estimate and control costs

items.item: The number of bytes a query reads is estimated before execution, and a query whose estimate exceeds maximum_bytes_billed fails without incurring a charge

at.step: A byte cap that fails before the charge, not after

items.item: Credit usage doubles with each warehouse size increase per full hour, but billing is per-second with a 60-second minimum, and warehouses auto-suspend when inactive and auto-resume on the next query

at.step: A warehouse that stops billing the moment nobody needs it

items.item: A resource monitor tracks warehouse credit usage and can alert, suspend standard warehouses, or disable Adaptive Warehouses at a threshold, but works for warehouses only, not serverless features

at.step: A warehouse that stops billing the moment nobody needs it

sources.source: Databricks: Attribute usage with serverless usage policies

items.item: A serverless usage policy attaches a tag to serverless activity, logged in billing records for budget attribution, applied automatically when a user has only one policy

at.step: A tag is not a cap

sources.source: Google Cloud: Spot VMs; Create and use Spot VMs

items.item: Spot VMs offer discounts up to 91% in exchange for preemption at any time; preemption sends a metadata signal, with a 120-second notice duration recommended, and a best-effort shutdown period up to 30 seconds

at.step: A steep discount, and the price of accepting it

items.item: A committed-use discount trades a 1- or 3-year spend or resource commitment for a discounted rate, with standard spend-based CUDs discounting until the hourly committed spend amount is met

at.step: A multi-year discount, and the flexibility it costs you

expert.by: self-review (make-topic session, builds every stage itself; see PROJECT_PLAN.md 'No subagents')

items.item: The hook's point is that a byte cap acts before the charge exists, not that on-demand billing is inherently dangerous; a learner should be able to name exactly what the cap checks (an estimate, before execution), not just that it 'stops bad queries'

at.step: One missing filter, one month of budget, gone

items.item: The predict step's correct answer is structural (refuses before the cost is incurred), not platform-specific; a learner should be able to separate a before-the-fact block from an after-the-fact alert before learning which vendor calls which mechanism what

at.step: Before the guardrails: which of these actually stop a cost, not just flag it?

items.item: The clustered-table caveat (estimate can exceed actual bytes billed) is disclosed in FACT-CHECK.md and SOURCES.md even though reel.tsx doesn't dedicate a full step to it, so a learner researching the real guardrail isn't misled into thinking the cap is always exact

at.step: A byte cap that fails before the charge, not after

items.item: The warehouse step's point is that auto-suspend and a resource monitor both actually act (suspend, disable), not merely notify; a learner who thinks a resource monitor only sends an email has missed that it can suspend a warehouse outright

at.step: A warehouse that stops billing the moment nobody needs it

items.item: The Databricks step is careful not to overstate what a budget policy does: it is attribution tagging, not a spending cap, and the topic says so explicitly rather than implying parity with BigQuery's or Snowflake's blocking mechanisms

at.step: A tag is not a cap

items.item: The spot-VM step states the 91% figure with its own 'up to' qualifier rather than as a guaranteed discount, and separates the metadata signal from the shutdown period rather than conflating the two timings

at.step: A steep discount, and the price of accepting it

items.item: The commitment break-even step reuses topic 10's own break-even-utilization method rather than inventing a new formula, and the illustrative rates are disclosed as illustrative in both examples.py's docstring and FACT-CHECK.md, not presented as real published prices

at.step: A multi-year discount, and the flexibility it costs you

items.item: The cost-regression step's point is that a dollar figure can fail a build exactly like any other regression check; a learner should be able to say what made the gate trip (a percentage increase over baseline), not just that 'cost matters'

at.step: A cost spike that fails the build, like any other regression

items.item: The final predict step's correct answer names the byte cap specifically because it's the only listed option that runs before the charge; a learner who picks the budget tag or the dashboard has conflated attribution or observation with actual prevention

at.step: Prove it

items.item: This topic cannot provision a real BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks or Compute Engine account in this sandbox; an expert reviewer should expect examples.py's disclosed structural simulation of each documented mechanism against synthetic data, not a live billing account
